newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ex-Irish p.m. Haughey seen named in payments probe.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Irish p.m. Haughey seen named in payments probe.

text.p: An inquiry into charges that a department store millionaire paid millions to Irish politicians opens on Monday amid reports that former prime minister Charles Haughey will be named as a recipient.

The Sunday Times joined a long list of Irish media in naming Haughey, a giant of the Irish political establishment, as the man who is alleged to have received more than a million punts ($1.6 million) from millionaire Ben Dunne.

The investigation is likely to stoke the fires under a smouldering election campaign pitting Prime Minister John Bruton's three-party coalition against the Fianna Fail opposition which Haughey once led.

Bertie Ahern, current Fianna Fail leader, told his annual party conference on Friday that he would not tolerate unethical behaviour by party members but said anyone named at the tribunal was innocent until proved guilty.

Haughey, prime minister four times between 1979 and 1992, has said nothing publicly apart from a one-line media denial through an unnamed source when the scandal burst last December and claimed its first political scalp.

Michael Lowry, a rising star in Bruton's Fine Gael party, resigned after admitting that Dunne paid for a quarter-million pound house rennovation. Lowry denied any impropriety but stepped down as transport minister.
The scandal raised calls for an overhaul of the way political parties are funded in Ireland and more openness in the links between big business and politics.

Dunne, from a family that owns one of Ireland's most succesful businesses, is expected to be among the first called to give evidence when the tribunal of inquiry begins at Dublin Castle. It could last several weeks.

According to the Sunday Times and other media, Haughey, who is to Irish politics what Margaret Thatcher was to Britain and Francois Mitterrand was to France, received the cash through intermediaries in 1989.
It said the money, paid in several instalments, ended up in an account in the Cayman Islands, which has strict secrecy laws protecting account holders.
Ahern, who has effectively launched his campaign although no election date has been set, denied reports that he had a bitter row with Haughey over Christmas after the allegations first surfaced.
He said he feared Bruton would allow the tribunal to name a leading Fianna Fail figure before adjourning to give Fine Gael an edge in the election campaign.

When a newspaper first broke the story, both Fine Gael and its junior coalition partner, the Labour party, admitted receiving small sums of cash from Dunne but said it was for election campaign purposes and was all accounted for.
The latest reports said an audit carried out by the Dunne family into its business finances showed that a "senior figure" in Fianna Fail had received 1.1 million pounds from Dunne.

Dunne was dropped from the family business in 1993 and, according to the Sunday Times, other members of the family tried to recover the money from Haughey in 1994. He denied having ever received it, the newspaper said.
